\title{The Round Complexity of Small Set Intersection}
\author{David P. Woodruff \\ IBM Almaden \\{\tt dpwoodru@us.ibm.com} \and Grigory Yaroslavtsev \\Penn State University\\{\tt grigory@cse.psu.edu}}
The set disjointness problem is one of the most fundamental and well-studied problems in communication complexity. In this problem
Alice and Bob hold sets $S, T \subseteq [n]$, respectively, and the goal is to decide if $S \cap T = \emptyset$. Reductions
from set disjointness are a canonical way of proving lower bounds in data stream algorithms, data structures, and
distributed computation. In these applications, often the set sizes $|S|$ and $|T|$ are bounded by a value $k$ which is
much smaller than $n$. This is referred
to as small set disjointness. A major restriction in the above applications is the number of rounds
that the protocol can make, which, e.g., translates to the number of passes in streaming applications. A fundamental question
is thus in understanding the round complexity of the small set disjointness problem. For an essentially equivalent problem,
called OR-Equality, Brody et. al showed that with $r$ rounds of communication, the randomized communication
$\Omega(k \ilog^r k)$, where$\ilog^r k$ denotes the $r$-th iterated logarithm function. Unfortunately their result
requires the error probability of the protocol to be $1/k^{\Theta(1)}$. Since na\"ive amplification of the
success probability of a protocol from constant to $1-1/k^{\Theta(1)}$
blows up the communication by a $\Theta(\log k)$ factor, this destroys their improvements over the well-known
lower bound of $\Omega(k)$ which holds for any number of rounds. They pose it as an open question
to achieve the same $\Omega(k \ilog^r k)$ lower bound for protocols with constant error probability.
We answer this open question by showing that the $r$-round randomized communication complexity of
${\sf OREQ}_{n,k}$, and thus also of small set disjointness, with {\it constant
error probability} is $\Omega(k \ilog^r k)$, asymptotically matching known upper bounds for ${\sf OREQ}_{n,k}$
Our techniques also have applications to sketching, where we qualitatively strengthen recent lower bounds
of Molinaro et. al for solving multiple instances of classical streaming problems.
One of the most well-studied problems in communication complexity is the disjointness function ${\sf DISJ}^n_k(S, T)$.
In this problem, Alice has an input set $S \subseteq [n]$ of size at most $k$, Bob has an input set $T \subseteq [n]$
of size at most $k$, and ${\sf DISJ}^n_k(S,T) = 1$ iff $|S \cap T| = 0$.
This problem, and its variants, has been used to prove a vast array of lower bounds for circuit complexity \cite{nw93},
data stream algorithms \cite{AMS99,BJKS04,CKS03}, proof complexity \cite{bps07}, game theory \cite{cs04, dn11, hm07, ns06},
the reader to the survey by Chattopadhyay and Pitassi \cite{cp10}.
A fundamental restriction in the above applications is the number of rounds
that the protocol can make, which translates to the number of passes in streaming applications.
H{\r a}stad and Wigderson \cite{hw07} showed that
$R({\sf DISJ}^n_k) = \Theta(k)$. The lower bound of $\Omega(k)$ follows by taking known lower bounds for set disjointness
without a cardinality restriction on $S$ and $T$, due to Kalysundaram and Schnitger \cite{ks92}, simplified by
Razborov \cite{r92} and Bar-Yossef et al. \cite{BJKS04}, and combining them with a padding argument.
The upper bound of $O(k)$ is due to a protocol given by H{\r a}stad and Wigderson, which they also remark was
years ago \cite{prw97}. In recent work by Braverman et. al \cite{bgpw12}, the authors
establish very tight bounds on the constant factor in the communication bounds for ${\sf DISJ}^n_k$,
namely, they show that the multi-round communication is $\frac{2}{\ln 2} k \pm o(k)$, though their result does not give a lower
bound in terms of the number of rounds.
It is also known that $R^{(1)}({\sf DISJ}^n_k) = \Theta(k \log k)$ \cite{bgmw12,DKS12},
though the complexity as a function
of the number $r$ of rounds for $r > 1$ is open. In an unpublished manuscript,
Jowhari et. al \cite{jst} show an upper bound of $R^{(r)}({\sf DISJ}^n_k) = O(k \ilog^r k)$.

We qualitatively improve all of the lower bounds in \cite{MWY13} using Theorem \ref{thm:augOrIndex}. The improvement is that
while \cite{MWY13} looked at solving multiple instances of various problems, such as $\ell_p$-estimation or inner product, and
showed lower bounds for protocols which solve all instances simultaneously, we obtain the same lower bounds even if
the protocol is just required to decide if {\it there exists a single instance among the multiple instances},
which has a certain property. This stems from the fact that in the communication problem we reduced from, instead
of requiring all $n$ instances of a problem to be solved, we only require solving the OR of $n$ instances. We discuss
the applications and improvements in more detail below.

Alice has $n$ vectors $\mathbf{v}^1, \mathbf{v}^2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}^n \in [\pm M]^d$, Bob has $n$ vectors $\mathbf{u}^1, \mathbf{u}^2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}^n \in [\pm M]^d$, and their goal is to compute (with probability at least $1 - \delta$) approximations $(1 \pm \epsilon) \|\mathbf{u}^i - \mathbf{v}^i\|_p$ to the $\ell_p$ distances \emph{for all} $i \in [n]$. Let $\ell_p(n, d, M, \epsilon)$ denote this problem.

Assume that $n$ is at least a sufficiently large constant and that $\epsilon$ is at most a sufficiently small constant. Also assume that there is a constant $\gamma > 0$ such that $d^{1 - \gamma} \ge \frac{1}{\epsilon^2} = \Omega(\log n)$. By replacing this problem with {\sf Augmented-OR-Index} we obtain the stronger version described above.
